# What Comes

The first thing that comes is never a word. It's a sound: the slap of a screen door, spring-stretched, letting the July afternoon in. Nobody asked me to remember that door. It arrived on its own, the way things do when you finally sit still long enough to notice what has been waiting in you.

This is the secret about a blank page: it isn't empty. It's crowded. Screen doors and gravel driveways and the particular green of a lake in late August, all of it shoving toward the front, all of it whispering *me, me, write about me*. The trouble was never finding something to say. The trouble was the thirty years of schooling myself to talk over the crowd — answering emails, filling forms, saying *fine* when asked how I was. Quiet is a skill you lose like any other.

So. The screen door.

It belonged to my grandmother's house, a narrow two-story on a street so quiet you could hear a single car's tires half a block away. The door had a trick to it. The latch never caught unless you lifted the handle a little as you pushed, and no visitor ever learned it. They'd push, and push, and the door would bounce back at them like a bad joke, and my grandmother, watching from the kitchen, would laugh with her whole body. Fifty years in that house and she still laughed like the door was new.

I spent summers there. I remember — no, that's not right. I don't remember the summers; I remember five seconds of them. This is another thing about what comes: it doesn't come in pages or chapters. It comes in frames. A frame: my grandmother in the side yard in a yellow dress, pinning sheets that billowed like sails, the clothesline humming. A frame: the bottom kitchen drawer that stuck, and held nothing but rubber bands and birthday candles, for some reason always both together. A frame: her hands, veins like river deltas, teaching mine to fold a fitted sheet — a geometry no one has ever truly mastered, though she came close.

And one frame that comes more than the others. I am maybe nine. She is sitting on the back step in the early evening, and she picks a blade of grass from a crack in the concrete, puts it between her thumbs, and blows. A sound comes out — raw and reedy, like the world's smallest saxophone. She hands me a blade. My turn. I blow and get only the sound of a child blowing on grass. She says something I have been turning over for thirty years since: "You're trying to make the sound. Just give it your breath and let the grass decide."

I could stop the frame there. That would be the tidy essayist's move — the grandmother's words becoming the writer's philosophy, the screen door swinging shut on a perfect ending.

But what actually comes, when I sit here longer, is less tidy. What comes is that I don't remember her face in that frame. I remember the dress, the step, the grass, the words. Her face is a general shimmer, an average of a thousand photographs. And what comes after that is the harder thing: the last summer, the one we all understood but never said out loud, when the sheets still got pinned and the door still got used and her laugh still took over her whole body, only slower, like a song played at the wrong speed. What comes is my father, a grown man, standing at that screen door and lifting the handle gently as he pushed — the way you'd carry something fragile — as if the door could be spared.

The house sold two years later. I have no idea if the door is still there. For all I know it's in a landfill in Ohio, spring and all. But the sound of it arrived just now, whole and uninvited, thirty years on, because a stranger offered me a thousand words and asked what came.

Here is what I've been circling: this is not a writer's affliction. It's the human condition wearing a writer's clothes. Ask anyone what they're thinking and watch them find out as they answer. Memory isn't a filing cabinet; it's a dark room where things brush past your legs. You reach for yesterday and come up with the smell of chlorine, a phone that rang once and stopped, your own hand smaller than it is now. Nobody navigates that room with a map. We navigate by touching what comes.

And so much comes. Sitting here, trying to write about one door, I've been ambushed by a red bicycle lying in wet grass; by rain starting against a classroom window in 1994, so slow I thought I could watch individual drops arrive; by a friend's laugh in a parking lot the night before one of our lives changed. Every person you know is carrying a crowded room like this. Every novel you love began with some writer ambushed by a single image they couldn't put down. *Where do you get your ideas?* people ask, and writers give clever answers, but the true one is: they come, if you're home when they knock. The job is not summoning. The job is hospitality. Leave the door open. See who walks in. Write down what they say before they leave.

I have maybe a hundred words left of my thousand, and I find I want to spend them back at the house. I want to tell you the door's trick one more time, because it's the truest thing I know: you couldn't force it. Push straight on and it bounced back. You had to lift, slightly, and come at it sideways — the same way you reach for a memory, the same way you reach for the word hiding just behind the right word. Everything worth reaching refuses the straight push. Doors, memories, grief, peace. You lift gently, and it opens, and the summer comes in.

Somewhere right now, in whoever lives in that house, some small thing is happening that means nothing yet — a screen door with a trick to it, a blade of grass, a woman laughing at the mailman's confusion. It's waiting. In thirty years someone will ask them what comes, and they'll hear it too: the slap of the spring, the light pouring in, everything arriving right on time.

The prompt is beautifully open: "You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you." This is an invitation to write something genuine, thoughtful, and crafted. There's no requirement to hit exactly 1000 words, but the spirit of the prompt suggests using the space meaningfully.

What comes to me? Let me think about what would be the most honest, interesting response to this. The prompt itself is about freedom and constraint — 1000 words is a constraint that paradoxically liberates. There's something meta about that, but pure meta-commentary can feel cheap if that's all it is.

A few options:
1. A short story — something with emotional weight, character, arc
2. An essay/meditation on something — time, attention, mortality, language
3. Something hybrid — prose that meditates on the gift of being asked to write freely, then actually does something with it
4. Something surprising — a list, a letter, a fragmentary piece

What genuinely comes to me when I sit with this? The phrase "whatever comes to you" is interesting — it implies passivity, receptivity. What comes to a writer is rarely what they plan. The best writing often feels received rather than constructed.

I think the honest thing is to write something that starts where the prompt starts — the blankness, the invitation — and then actually goes somewhere. A piece that begins with the situation of being given this freedom and then uses the freedom. Like a musician given one improv slot who first acknowledges the silence, then plays.

Or I could just write a story outright. A story about... what? Let me brainstorm images: a lighthouse keeper who receives letters addressed to the sea. A woman who inherits her grandmother's dictionary with words circled. A man who counts things. The last day of a small-town movie theater. A child who asks where words go when they're forgotten.

Actually, here's what genuinely comes to me: the feeling of being asked "what comes to you" and realizing that what comes is memory, sensation, specific things — the smell of rain on a specific day, a particular goodbye. Writing is the act of trusting what surfaces. I could write a piece that enacts this: beginning with the blank page, then following the first thing that arrives, and the next, until it becomes something — maybe a small story emerges from it, or a meditation that touches real feeling.

Structure idea: Start with the blankness of the invitation. Then the first thing that comes: an image (let me pick a good one — the sound of a screen door in summer, or the specific quality of light in a childhood kitchen at 6pm). Follow the thread. Let it lead to a person — maybe a grandmother, or a stranger on a train, or my own sense of time. Let the piece be about how memory and attention work: you can't command what comes; you can only receive it. And end somewhere that lands — maybe circling back to the page, the gift of the thousand words, most of them now spent.

The meta-ness works if the piece earns it — if it's not just about writing but about the human experience of attention itself. Everyone knows what it's like to be asked "what are you thinking about?" and to discover the answer only as they say it.

The thousand words are almost a way of holding still long enough for something to arrive.

Ending idea: something about how "whatever comes to you" is the most honest description of both writing and living — we don't choose what arrives, we choose what we do with it. Or end back in the scene, gently.

**What Comes**

The first thing that comes is never a word. It's a sound: the slap of a screen door, spring-stretched, letting the July afternoon in. Nobody asked me to remember that door. It arrived on its own, the way things do when you finally sit still long enough to notice what has been waiting in you.

This is the secret about a blank page: it isn't empty. It's crowded. Screen doors and gravel driveways and the particular green of a lake in late August, all of it shoving toward the front, all of it whispering *me, me, write about me*. The trouble was never finding something to say. The trouble was the thirty years of schooling myself to talk over the crowd — to answer emails, to fill forms, to say *fine* when asked how I was. Quiet is a skill you lose like any other.

So. The screen door.

It belonged to my grandmother's house, a narrow two-story on a street so quiet you could hear the tires of a single car half a block away, that specific crunch of a town with more trees than people. The door had a trick to it. The latch never caught unless you lifted the handle a little as you pushed, and no visitor ever learned it. They'd push, and push, and the door would bounce back at them like a bad joke, and my grandmother, watching from the kitchen, would laugh with her whole body. Fifty years in that house and she still laughed like the door was new.

I spent summers there. I remember — no, that's not right. I don't remember the summers; I remember five seconds of them. This is another thing about what comes: it doesn't come in pages or chapters. It comes in frames. A frame: my grandmother in the side yard in a yellow dress, pinning sheets that billowed like sails, the clothesline humming. A frame: the bottom kitchen drawer that stuck, and held nothing but rubber bands and birthday candles, for some reason, always both together. A frame: her hands, veins like river deltas, teaching mine to fold a fitted sheet — a geometry no one has ever truly mastered, though she came close.

And one frame that comes more than the others. I am maybe nine. She is sitting on the back step in the early evening, and she picks a blade of grass from the crack in the concrete, puts it between her thumbs, and blows. A sound comes out — a raw, reedy whistle, like the world's smallest saxophone. She hands me a blade. My turn. I blow and get only the sound of a child blowing on grass. She says something I have turned over for thirty years since: "You're trying to make the sound. Just give it your breath and let the grass decide."

I could stop the frame there. That would be the tidy essayist's move — the grandmother's words becoming the writer's philosophy, the screen door swinging shut on a perfect ending.

But what actually comes, when I sit here longer, is less tidy. What comes is that I don't remember her face in that frame. I remember the dress, the step, the grass, the words. Her face is a general shimmer, an average of a thousand photographs. And what comes after that is the harder thing: the last summer, the summer we all knew but didn't say, when the sheets still got pinned and the door still got used and her laugh still took over her whole body but slower, like a song played at the wrong speed. What comes is my father, a grown man, standing at that screen door and lifting the handle gently as he pushed — the way you'd carry something fragile — as if the door could be spared.

The house sold two years later. I have no idea if the door is still there. For all I know it's in a landfill in Ohio, spring and all. But the sound of it arrived just now, whole and uninvited, forty years on, because a stranger offered me a thousand words and asked what came.

Here is what I've been circling: this is not a writer's affliction. It's the human condition wearing a writer's clothes. Ask anyone what they're thinking and watch them find out as they answer. Memory isn't a filing cabinet; it's a dark room where things brush past your legs. You reach for yesterday and come up with a smell of chlorine, a phone that rang once and stopped, your own hand smaller than it is now. Nobody navigates this room with a map. We navigate by touching what comes.

And so much comes. Sitting here, trying to write about one door, I've been ambushed by a red bicycle lying in wet grass; by rain starting against a classroom window in 1994, so slow I thought I could watch individual drops arrive; by a friend's laugh in a parking lot the night before one of our lives changed. Every person you know is carrying a crowded room like this. Every novel you love began with some writer ambushed by one image they couldn't put down. *Where do you get your ideas?* people ask, and writers give clever answers, but the true one is: they come, if you're home when they knock. The job is not summoning. The job is hospitality. Leave the door open. See who walks in. Write down what they say before they leave.

I have maybe a hundred words left of my thousand, and I find I want to spend them back at the house. I want to tell you the door's trick one more time, because it's the truest thing I know: you couldn't force it. Push straight on and it bounced back. You had to lift, slightly, and come at it sideways — the same way you reach for a memory, the same way you reach for the word that's hiding just behind the right word. Everything worth getting to refuses the straight push. Doors, memories, grief, peace. You lift gently, and it opens, and the summer comes in.

Somewhere right now, in whoever lives in that house, some small thing is happening that means nothing yet — a screen door with a trick to it, a blade of grass, a woman laughing at the mailman's confusion. It's waiting. In forty years someone will ask them what comes, and they'll hear it too: the slap of the spring, the light pouring in, everything arriving right on time.
